title: Praise and Encouragement Are Not the Same Thing
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece distinguishes praise, which approves of results already achieved, from encouragement, which expresses belief in someone's capability before the results are in. It grants that praise is effective but argues it carries baggage: too much erodes intrinsic motivation, breeds dependence on approval and puts the leader on a pedestal. Encouragement, by contrast, drives people to work through their own effort, promotes self-evaluation and shifts attention away from the leader. The author concludes that the best leaders consciously shift from less praise to more encouragement. Three paired rewordings show the move, converting a statement of the leader's pride into a prompt for the person to own and explain their success.
points: Praise's cost is that people come to depend on approval and put more weight on pleasing the leader than on the work itself.
Encouragement signals confidence in capability before results exist, which builds the resolve to perform.
Encouragement redirects focus from the leader to the team member and invites self-evaluation.
The paired rewrites (for example turning 'You did a great job' into 'Tell me how you achieved so much') give leaders a concrete script for the shift.
quotes: Too much praise robs people of the intrinsic motivation to achieve great outcomes for personal satisfaction. Team members can quickly become dependent on praise for everything they do.

This actually diminishes performance over time as they crave more and more praise, placing more emphasis on approval than on the work itself. It also places leaders on a pedestal from which they are expected to dole out ever more praise like some pied piper.
Encouragement, on the other hand, tells others the leader believes they have the capability to achieve. Encouragement provides support and confidence before the results are in.

In contrast to praise, encouragement inspires people to do more through their own effort and promotes self-evaluation. It emboldens others to do great work without focusing attention on the leader. If praise is the candy leaders hand out, encouragement is the rocket fuel leaders inject to strengthen resolve.

I’m proud of what you have accomplished!” becomes “You’ve worked hard. You must be very proud of yourself.” “You did a great job on that assignment!” turns into “Tell me how you achieved so much on that assignment.

On the face of it, praise and encouragement seem almost interchangeable, but there is a marked difference between them. The best leaders rely more heavily on encouragement than they do praise because they understand the importance of getting people to lift themselves up with just a little help from a few choice words.
